title: The Texas City Disaster of 1947
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the 1947 Texas City disaster, the largest industrial disaster in US history. On April 16, 1947, the Grand Camp, loaded with ammonium nitrate fertilizer, caught fire in the Texas City port while docked beside the High Flyer (also carrying ammonium nitrate and sulfur) and the Wilson B. Keene. Firefighters and a captain's decision to pump steam into the holds worsened the fire; hatches blew off, onlookers gathered, and the Grand Camp exploded at 9:12 a.m. The blast leveled the port, killed the entire 28-member volunteer fire department, and sent debris and a tidal wave inland. The High Flyer later exploded the next morning. Death toll was about 581 with 113 never found; casualties and property losses are discussed, along with recovery, the unidentified victims' memorial, and comparisons to the 2005 BP Texas City refinery explosion and the 2020 Beirut ammonium nitrate explosion. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from Ryan Peschel about the show's closing transition.
topics: largest industrial disaster in US history

segments.title: Introduction and Texas City background
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode as the largest US industrial disaster and describe Texas City as a petrochemical port town, its founding, and its wartime and postwar port operations under looser civilian oversight.
topics: largest industrial disaster in US history

segments.title: Cargo ships and ammonium nitrate
segments.summary: The three Liberty ships at the docks (Grand Camp, High Flyer, Wilson B. Keene) are described along with their cargo of ammonium nitrate fertilizer in paper sacks, sulfur, and other goods. The hosts explain ammonium nitrate's properties, including its sensitivity to moisture and heat and how it decomposes explosively.

segments.title: Fire aboard the Grand Camp and steam firefighting
segments.summary: The fire aboard the Grand Camp starts around 8 a.m. on April 16, and the captain battens the hatches and pumps in steam, a method that heats the cargo and makes things worse. Hatch covers blow off around 8:30 a.m., and colorful smoke draws hundreds of onlookers.

segments.title: The initial explosion and its effects
segments.summary: Firefighters and a tugboat arrive, but the heat defeats hoses. The Grand Camp explodes at 9:12 a.m., hurling a ship's pieces and anchors, flattening chemical plants and the port warehouses, killing the 28-member fire department and onlookers, and sending a tidal wave inland. The blast was felt as far as Louisiana and Denver.

segments.title: High Flyer fire and second explosion
segments.summary: The High Flyer, loaded with ammonium nitrate and sulfur, catches fire and drifts into the Wilson B. Keene. Crew members stay aboard until forced off by smoke. Attempts to tow the ship from its berth fail, and it explodes the next morning, April 17, sinking the Wilson B. Keene.

segments.title: Death toll, rescue, recovery and memorial
segments.summary: The official death toll is close to 600 with 113 never found; casualties were in the thousands. Victims were taken to Galveston, the high school gym became a field hospital and morgue, and Boy Scouts helped. Sixty-one or sixty-three unidentified victims were buried in a memorial park after a large funeral procession. Property losses were about $100 million.

segments.title: Aftermath, regulation and later explosions
segments.summary: The city rebuilt, and the hosts note that regulation followed. They compare the disaster to the 2020 Beirut ammonium nitrate explosion and then describe the 2005 BP Texas City refinery explosion, which was linked to cut safety and a pickup truck engine ignition.

segments.title: Listener mail from Ryan Peschel
segments.summary: Ryan Peschel writes about mistakenly believing Josh's closing word-transition was drawn from a secret list of words, and both hosts respond playfully.
